screens.title: Performing a Predictive Site Survey
screens.narratorSegment: Predictive site surveys are a planning-first approach that let you model radio frequency behavior from floor plans and material properties. In this lesson you will learn why a predictive survey is usually the first step in a WLAN design, how to import and scale a plan accurately, how to define material attenuation so your simulation matches reality, and how to place virtual access points to meet coverage and capacity goals. We'll also show how to read heatmaps for RSSI, SNR, and estimated throughput and use those results to iterate toward a balanced design. A predictive survey saves time and cost by reducing hardware trial-and-error, but it depends on accurate inputs: scale, material values, and realistic client density assumptions. For example, using a mis-scaled drawing can make an AP appear to cover a hallway that in reality is twice as long, producing poor outcomes. By the end of this chapter you will be able to set up a survey plan, apply sensible attenuation values, place virtual APs for coverage and capacity targets, and interpret heatmaps to find gaps and over-provisioning. Keep an eye out for common mistakes like ignoring SNR or over-designing with too many APs; addressing those early keeps your design practical. What is one measurement on your floor plans you can check now to avoid a scaling mistake?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Interpretation
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives screen focuses on applying the predictive survey skills and interpreting outputs. You will learn to place virtual APs both for coverage and for capacity-driven designs, and to use heatmaps for RSSI, SNR and throughput to check whether performance targets are met. For coverage-driven placement, the goal is a minimum RSSI target across the service area, for example a value suitable for voice. For capacity-driven placement you will learn to create smaller cells by reducing transmit power and placing APs closer together, which helps in high-density rooms such as conference spaces. You will also practice basic channel planning rules such as non-overlapping channels in 2.4 GHz and mindful channel separation and DFS considerations in 5 GHz. Finally, you will validate your design iteratively: place APs, generate heatmaps, inspect for red zones, and refine until the simulated results meet requirements. Knowing how to interpret SNR and throughput prevents common mistakes where good RSSI does not mean good performance. Consider which area in your environment needs capacity rather than simple coverage; that distinction guides AP count and placement.

screens.title: What is a Predictive Site Survey?
screens.narratorSegment: A predictive site survey is a software-driven simulation that models Wi‑Fi signal propagation using a scaled floor plan and material attenuation values. The technique lets you approximate where signal will reach, how strong it will be, and where capacity limits may appear, all before any hardware is installed. This matters because it reduces the expensive cycle of installing APs, testing, and reworking placement. A good predictive survey starts with accurate inputs: the scaled drawing and realistic attenuation settings for walls, glass, and metallic obstacles. For example, a drywall partition will typically attenuate a 5 GHz signal by only a few decibels, while a thick concrete wall can cause an order of magnitude more loss. A common misconception is to treat a predictive survey as a final truth rather than a model; it is a tool that is only as accurate as the data you provide. Use predictive surveys to estimate AP count, initial placement, and where to focus a follow-up physical verification. In practice this means you can identify likely red zones on a heatmap, refine AP locations or power, and produce a design that requires fewer on-site adjustments. Ask yourself: what local construction features could change the model’s accuracy at your site?

keyIdea.text: A simulation using scaled plans and material losses to predict RF behavior and guide AP placement before installation.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › What is a Predictive Site Survey?
Core Concept

Predictive Site Survey

A model-based survey that predicts RF propagation using scaled floor plans and material attenuation.

Why use it?
  • Saves time by reducing physical trial-and-error.
  • Helps estimate AP count, placement, and power settings.
  • Highlights potential coverage gaps before installation.
Common misconception

The model isn't absolute truth; it reflects the inputs. Incorrect scaling or wrong material losses make results unreliable.

Concrete example

Using a scaled CAD plan and assigning a 12 dB loss for a concrete exterior wall, you can predict a coverage gap behind that wall and plan a second AP rather than increasing transmit power on the first.

Key Takeaway

Predictive surveys guide design decisions and reduce on-site rework, but only when scale and material inputs are accurate.

screens.title: Importing and Scaling Floor Plans
screens.narratorSegment: Importing and scaling a floor plan is the foundation of every predictive survey. Begin by obtaining the best available drawing: a CAD file or a high-resolution image. When you import the file into survey software, you must set the real-world scale by measuring a known dimension on the plan, such as a 10 meter exterior wall, and inputting that length so the software can convert pixels or drawing units to meters. The guidance in the source material is clear: check at least two known distances after scaling to confirm accuracy. Common mistakes include using an unscaled or low-resolution image and assuming the drawing is to scale without verifying. Always validate your scale by measuring two independent dimensions—this catches distortions or different drawing scales across floors. If you discover errors, re-import or correct the scale before placing any virtual APs, since AP separation, coverage predictions, and channel planning depend on true distances. Finally, label key rooms and features so you can later map capacity requirements to specific areas. After scaling correctly, you can draw walls and obstacles and begin assigning material properties with confidence. What two distances can you verify on your next plan?

keyIdea.title: Scaling steps
keyIdea.text: Import a CAD/image, set scale using a known dimension, and verify using at least two independent measurements.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Importing and Scaling Floor Plans
Process Flow

Import & scale the plan accurately

A reliable base map is essential for meaningful heatmaps and AP placement.

Step-by-step
  1. Obtain CAD or high-resolution image of the floor.
  2. Import into the survey tool and choose drawing units.
  3. Set scale by measuring a known dimension and entering its real length.
  4. Verify scale by checking at least two independent distances.
  5. Label important rooms and features for later capacity mapping.
Common mistakes
  • Assuming a drawing is already scaled without verification.
  • Using low-resolution images that hide small but important features.
Example check

If the plan shows an exterior wall labeled 20 meters, set that segment to 20 m in the tool. Then verify an interior room width or corridor length to confirm scaling consistency.

Key Takeaway

Scaling errors propagate to everything else. Verify at least two known distances before modeling materials or placing APs.

screens.title: Material Attenuation
screens.narratorSegment: Material attenuation is the reduction in RF signal strength as radio waves pass through walls, glass, doors, furniture, or metallic structures. Different materials produce different losses. The chapter gives useful examples: a drywall office partition may attenuate a 5 GHz signal by around 3 to 5 dB, while a thick concrete wall often causes 10 to 15 dB loss. The hands-on scenario uses 12 dB for an exterior concrete wall and 4 dB for a drywall partition to illustrate how these values affect coverage predictions. It’s important to choose values that match local construction practices and, when possible, validate them with physical measurements. In survey software you typically draw walls and assign a material type from a library or custom values. A common misconception is to assume all walls are the same; a reinforced concrete shear wall can create a major coverage gap if modeled as a light partition. Another pitfall is to ignore metallic obstructions like shelving or elevator shafts which can present very high attenuation. Accurate material mapping helps your model reveal where extra APs will actually be needed rather than guessing later on-site. Which material near your site could change a predicted heatmap the most?

keyIdea.title: Material mapping
keyIdea.text: Assign realistic dB losses to walls and obstructions so simulations approximate real-world signal paths.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Material Attenuation
Definition

Material Attenuation

Assign dB losses to represent how materials reduce signal strength and shape coverage.

Common values
  • Drywall partition (5 GHz): ~3–5 dB
  • Thick concrete wall: ~10–15 dB
  • Metallic obstructions (elevator, shelving): much higher loss—treat with caution
Modeling tips
  • Use the software library but customize values if local construction differs.
  • Draw walls, doors, and windows so their locations affect heatmaps correctly.
Pitfall

Treating all partitions the same will produce misleading coverage. Validate high-loss features like shear walls or large metal objects in your model.

Example

In the sample office scenario use 12 dB for exterior concrete walls and 4 dB for interior drywall partitions to see how these losses change predicted RSSI across rooms.

Key Takeaway

Material values are a major input — get them right or validate them physically when possible.

screens.title: Drawing Walls and Obstacles on the Plan
screens.narratorSegment: After scaling the floor plan, the next step is to draw and tag the building elements that affect radio propagation. Draw exterior and interior walls, doors, windows, elevator shafts and large metallic fixtures, then assign the material type and its attenuation value. This may be done by selecting a wall tool and tracing each wall segment to match the plan. Be deliberate: a missing shear wall or metallic storage rack can produce large unpredicted losses. Also include doors and glass where their lower attenuation impacts the heatmap. Many survey tools provide a library of materials with default dB losses; use these as a starting point but adjust to reflect local building practice — the chapter warns that regional construction differences matter. After drawing, run an initial simulation to confirm the heatmap behavior looks sensible: broad open areas should show larger coverage footprints, and thick walls should create distinct signal shadows. If results look implausible, re-check scale and material assignments. This step bridges the static floor plan and the dynamic RF model; accuracy here is what lets you trust subsequent AP placement and capacity estimates. Which structural element on your plan would you mark first and why?

keyIdea.text: Trace walls and major obstructions and assign material types so the simulation can show realistic shadows and gaps.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Drawing Walls and Obstacles
Process Flow

Draw structural elements and assign materials

Make the plan an RF-aware model by tracing walls and tagging materials.

Steps to follow
  1. Trace exterior walls and assign concrete where appropriate.
  2. Trace interior partitions and assign drywall or other material types.
  3. Add doors, windows, elevator shafts and large metallic objects.
  4. Label rooms for capacity planning and user expectations.
Validation

Run an initial simulation and look for sensible signal shadows and coverage patterns. Implausible results often point to scaling or material assignment errors.

Example

If a heavy metal shelving unit sits in a storage room, add it as a high-attenuation object rather than leaving it blank. The heatmap will then show a localized shadow where signal is reduced.

Key Takeaway

Careful drawing of obstacles translates directly to realistic heatmaps and correct AP placement decisions.

screens.title: Virtual AP Placement — Coverage-Driven
screens.narratorSegment: Coverage-driven placement aims to ensure a minimum RSSI across the desired coverage area. Start by defining your RSSI target, for example a value suitable for voice, and then place virtual access points to meet that floor. After placing an AP, the software will generate a heatmap showing predicted RSSI; use that to identify areas below the target. Adjust AP location and transmit power to expand coverage where needed. A common mistake is to rely solely on transmit power increases to reach a distant area; this can create greater cell overlap and increase co-channel interference. Instead, move APs or add another AP in problem areas if the building structure blocks signals. For open areas you can often achieve coverage with fewer APs, while partitioned spaces may require additional APs near high-attenuation walls. The chapter emphasizes iterative refinement: place APs, check heatmaps, refine positions, and repeat until the coverage target is met without excessive overlap. Remember to keep SNR and throughput considerations in mind — good RSSI alone is not the whole picture. After you think coverage is solved, generate SNR and throughput heatmaps to verify real-world usability.

keyIdea.title: Coverage rule
keyIdea.text: Design to a minimum RSSI target and iterate placement rather than only increasing transmit power.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Virtual AP Placement — Coverage
Core Concept

Coverage-driven AP placement

Place APs to meet a minimum RSSI target across the area and iterate based on heatmap feedback.

Action steps
  1. Set a minimum RSSI target for the site.
  2. Place APs and generate an RSSI heatmap.
  3. Move or add APs where heatmap shows values below the target.
  4. Re-run heatmap until coverage target is met with moderate overlap.
Misconception

Boosting power is not a universal fix. It can increase co-channel interference and reduce overall performance if not paired with placement adjustments.

Example

If a classroom shows RSSI below the target, place an additional AP nearer to the classroom or move the original AP to a more central position, rather than simply increasing transmit power.

Key Takeaway

Target RSSI first, then iterate AP placement and power. Validate with SNR and throughput heatmaps afterward.

screens.title: Coverage vs Capacity Placement
screens.narratorSegment: Coverage-driven and capacity-driven placement address different problems. Coverage placement aims for signal everywhere by meeting a minimum RSSI, useful in general office spaces or hallways. Capacity placement focuses on areas with many concurrent users where throughput per user matters, such as conference rooms. For capacity, you often place multiple APs closer together and reduce their transmit power to create smaller cells. This allows more APs to operate in proximity without overwhelming co-channel interference and helps distribute clients across access points. The chapter highlights that capacity-driven designs require careful attention to power and channel planning, and that tools can accept client density inputs to optimize AP count. A common error is to rely on a single AP to cover a dense area simply because its RSSI meets the target; in that case throughput and client distribution will suffer. Another pitfall is over-designing: too many APs can increase co-channel interference and reduce overall performance. The right strategy balances cell size, transmit power, and channel separation to meet both coverage and capacity where they matter most. Which of your spaces is likely to need capacity-focused placement?

keyIdea.title: Placement contrast
keyIdea.text: Coverage optimizes RSSI across area; capacity optimizes user throughput by creating smaller cells and distributing load.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Coverage vs Capacity Placement
Comparison

Coverage-driven vs Capacity-driven

Choose the strategy depending on whether your priority is area coverage or number of supported users and throughput.

Coverage-driven
  • Goal: minimum RSSI across the service area.
  • Fewer APs, higher power may suffice in open areas.
  • Validate with RSSI heatmap and SNR checks.
Capacity-driven
  • Goal: serve high client density with acceptable throughput per user.
  • Place APs closer together and reduce power to form smaller cells.
  • Use client density inputs and channel planning to avoid interference.
Example

A conference room expected to host 50 users should be capacity-designed: several APs, lower power, and careful channel planning rather than one high-power AP that only meets RSSI.

Key Takeaway

Decide whether coverage or capacity drives each area, then tailor AP count, placement, and power to that need.

screens.title: Channel Planning Basics
screens.narratorSegment: Channel planning reduces co-channel interference and improves overall network performance. In 2.4 GHz the standard practice is to use the three non-overlapping channels — 1, 6 and 11 — to avoid adjacent-channel overlap. In 5 GHz and 6 GHz there are many more channels available, but you still need to ensure sufficient channel separation and be mindful of DFS channel behavior. The survey software typically provides initial channel assignment suggestions during predictive placement, but you should review and adjust them based on AP density and expected client channel use. A simple pitfall is to assume more APs means you can ignore channel planning; in fact, more APs make proper channel separation more important. When you design capacity-driven areas with smaller cells, lower transmit power helps, but you must coordinate channel assignments carefully to avoid multiple APs on the same channel in overlapping cells. Keep in mind that predictive tools can estimate interference but they cannot predict every external source — plan for some on-site verification and tuning after deployment. Which channel plan would you start with for a mixed 2.4 and 5 GHz deployment?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Channel Planning Basics
Core Concept

Channel planning essentials

Assign channels to minimize interference and preserve capacity in dense environments.

2.4 GHz

Prefer the three non-overlapping channels 1, 6 and 11 to avoid adjacent channel overlap in denser AP deployments.

5 GHz and 6 GHz

More channels exist, but ensure separation and be mindful of DFS channels which may require special handling.

Power & cells

When creating smaller cells for capacity, lower AP power and careful channel assignment help reduce co-channel interference.

Practical note

Let the tool suggest initial channels, then review channel reuse and DFS constraints before finalizing the design.

Key Takeaway

Channel planning is a necessary complement to AP placement; misconfigured channels can undo careful placement choices.

screens.title: Predictive Heatmaps Explained
screens.narratorSegment: Predictive heatmaps are the primary outputs of a predictive site survey. They visualize metrics such as RSSI, SNR, estimated throughput, coverage by AP, and predicted interference. RSSI maps show raw signal strength and help you identify areas below your minimum target. SNR maps reveal signal quality — even if RSSI looks good, a low SNR means performance will be poor due to noise. Throughput maps give an estimate of achievable data rates and are key for capacity validation. Coverage-by-AP maps show which AP will serve each area and help detect cell boundaries and roaming behavior. Some tools can also estimate co-channel interference based on channel assignments. Interpreting heatmaps is a skill: look for red or yellow zones that show low signal or marginal quality, and inspect where cell overlap is excessive or insufficient. A common error is to stop after correcting RSSI without checking SNR and throughput; the network may appear covered yet still perform poorly. Always iterate: adjust APs, rerun heatmaps, and balance coverage and capacity until all critical areas meet their performance targets. After that, validate on site where real-world noise and unexpected obstacles may differ from the model.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Predictive Heatmaps Explained
Core Concept

Heatmaps: RSSI, SNR, Throughput

Read multiple heatmap types together to understand predicted performance and user experience.

RSSI (Signal)

Shows predicted signal level; used to find coverage gaps relative to your RSSI floor.

SNR (Quality)

Indicates signal-to-noise ratio; low SNR means performance will suffer even if RSSI is acceptable.

Throughput

Estimates achievable data rates and validates capacity assumptions against client density targets.

Interpretation tip

Look for red zones showing poor RSSI or SNR, check whether they align with high-loss materials, and decide whether to move APs or add new ones to fix the problem.

Key Takeaway

Use heatmaps together — RSSI, SNR and throughput — to make balanced design decisions and avoid false confidence in signal strength alone.

screens.title: Iterative Design: Place, Check, Refine
screens.narratorSegment: Predictive surveys are iterative. After you place virtual APs and set materials, generate heatmaps and inspect for coverage holes, low SNR areas, or excessive overlap. If you see a red zone behind a heavy wall, the correct action is often to add another AP on the blocked side rather than merely increasing transmit power on existing APs, which can create interference. When an area shows marginal RSSI, try moving an AP a small distance, adjusting height, or changing power to see how the heatmap changes. For capacity concerns, create smaller cells with closer AP spacing and reduced power, and verify throughput maps for user-area targets. Keep channel planning in mind: as you add APs, review channel assignments to avoid co-channel interference. A common pitfall is over-designing — adding too many APs can reduce overall performance. The iteration loop is simple: place APs, run RSSI, SNR and throughput heatmaps, inspect results, adjust materials/placement/power, and repeat until requirements are met across all critical areas. Finally, document your plan and mark locations for physical verification after deployment to confirm the model against the real environment.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Iterative Design: Place, Check, Refine
Process Flow

Iterative refinement of AP layout

Converge on a design by repeating placement, simulation, and adjustments.

Loop
  1. Place APs and set power.
  2. Generate RSSI, SNR and throughput heatmaps.
  3. Identify gaps, overlaps, and low-quality zones.
  4. Adjust placement, power, or add APs and repeat.
Practical rule

Prefer adding APs to cover blocked areas rather than solely raising power, and watch for over-provisioning that increases interference.

Documentation

Record final AP locations, power, and channel plan, and mark areas for physical verification after deployment.

Example

If an area behind a concrete wall shows red on the RSSI map, add a virtual AP on that side and re-run heatmaps to ensure coverage and acceptable SNR.

Key Takeaway

Iterate deliberately: small changes, re-simulate, and avoid the temptation to over-power or over-deploy APs.

screens.title: Activity — Predictive AP Placement for a Small Office
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the chapter's sample scenario: a small rectangular office 20 meters by 10 meters with two long exterior concrete walls and two interior drywall partitions creating two 10 by 10 meter rooms. The requirement is a minimum RSSI of -65 dBm across the office. Start with floor plan import and scaling: import the plan image or CAD into your survey software and set the scale using the 20 meter exterior wall. Confirm scale by measuring the room width as a second check. Next, define materials. Draw the two exterior walls as concrete with 12 dB attenuation and the two interior partitions as drywall with 4 dB attenuation, matching the assumption in the scenario. Add labels for each 10x10 room. For initial AP placement assume a standard 802.11ax AP on the 5 GHz band with an omnidirectional pattern. Place a virtual AP near the center of each 10x10 room to start and generate an RSSI heatmap. Inspect for areas below -65 dBm; if one room shows a weak corner near the concrete wall, move the AP slightly toward that corner or add a third AP in the affected area rather than raising power. Finally, run SNR and throughput predictions to confirm capacity. This step-by-step approach mirrors how you would use a predictive tool in practice and prepares you to validate results on site.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Activity — Small Office Plan
Hands-on Activity

Predictive Survey Plan for Small Office

Follow the steps to practice import, material definition, and virtual AP placement for a 20m × 10m office.

1. Floor Plan Import & Scaling
  1. Import CAD or image of the 20×10 office.
  2. Set scale using a 20 m exterior wall and verify using a 10 m room width.
2. Material Definition
  • Mark exterior walls as concrete, attenuation = 12 dB.
  • Mark interior partitions as drywall, attenuation = 4 dB.
3. Initial AP Placement

Place a 5 GHz 802.11ax AP with an omnidirectional pattern in each 10×10 room center. Generate RSSI heatmap and check for areas below -65 dBm.

4. Refine & Validate

If a red zone appears near the concrete wall, add an AP on that side or move the AP closer instead of increasing power. Run SNR and throughput maps to confirm performance.

Key Takeaway

Follow the import-scale-define-place-iterate cycle to turn the scenario into a validated predictive design you can test on-site.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Assessment Items
screens.narratorSegment: This screen covers common mistakes and offers assessment items to check your understanding. A frequent error in predictive surveys is neglecting scaling: if the floor plan is not scaled accurately, every placement and distance-based decision will be wrong. The recommended corrective action when you see a deep red zone behind a concrete wall is to add another AP on the blocked side, not to increase transmit power or falsify material types. Another mistake is focusing solely on RSSI while ignoring SNR and throughput; good signal strength does not guarantee usable performance if noise is high. Over-design is also common: adding too many APs without channel coordination increases co-channel interference and can reduce real throughput. To assess mastery, use the two provided questions: first, when a red zone appears behind a concrete wall, the correct action is to add another AP in that red zone; second, the critical first step after loading a floor plan is to scale it using a known real-world dimension. These checks reinforce that accurate inputs and targeted fixes produce reliable predictive designs. After reading this, consider which mistake you are most likely to make on your next design and how you will guard against it.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Common Mistakes & Assessment
Assessment & Pitfalls

Avoid these common errors

Use the following quick checks and the sample questions to validate your approach.

Top mistakes
  • Failing to scale the floor plan before placing APs.
  • Relying on RSSI alone and ignoring SNR or throughput.
  • Over-designing with too many APs and causing interference.
Quick assessments
  1. If a red zone appears behind a concrete wall, add another AP in the red zone rather than increasing transmit power.
  2. After importing a floor plan, the first critical step is to scale it using a known dimension so all distances are accurate.
Example explanation

Increasing transmit power to overcome a high-loss wall often increases interference and rarely solves the root cause. Adding a localized AP is the recommended solution in simulation and practice.

Key Takeaway

Use assessment items to test designs: scale first, then model materials, and prefer AP placement fixes over power increases for blocked zones.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: Here are the key concepts to keep in mind. First, a predictive site survey models RF propagation with scaled floor plans and material attenuation so you can plan AP placement before installing hardware. Following that sequence helps you catch the biggest errors early and focus your design efforts on the inputs that matter most. fullNarratorScript:
Predictive site surveys are a planning-first approach that let you model radio frequency behavior from floor plans and material properties. In this lesson you will learn why a predictive survey is usually the first step in a WLAN design, how to import and scale a plan accurately, how to define material attenuation so your simulation matches reality, and how to place virtual access points to meet coverage and capacity goals. We'll also show how to read heatmaps for RSSI, SNR, and estimated throughput and use those results to iterate toward a balanced design. A predictive survey saves time and cost by reducing hardware trial-and-error, but it depends on accurate inputs: scale, material values, and realistic client density assumptions. For example, using a mis-scaled drawing can make an AP appear to cover a hallway that in reality is twice as long, producing poor outcomes. By the end of this chapter you will be able to set up a survey plan, apply sensible attenuation values, place virtual APs for coverage and capacity targets, and interpret heatmaps to find gaps and over-provisioning. Keep an eye out for common mistakes like ignoring SNR or over-designing with too many APs; addressing those early keeps your design practical. What is one measurement on your floor plans you can check now to avoid a scaling mistake?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the predictive survey methodology and why it is a foundational step for WLAN design, import and scale floor plans accurately in survey software, identify and assign realistic attenuation values to building materials, and place virtual access points to meet coverage and capacity targets. Each objective ties a practical skill to a validation milestone. For example, accurately scaling a floor plan means you can measure distances and place APs with confidence; a proven habit is to check at least two known distances such as exterior wall lengths or room widths. Defining material attenuation links construction knowledge to RF modeling; using appropriate dB values for drywall or concrete prevents surprise dead zones in simulations. Finally, virtual AP placement is where coverage and capacity requirements meet; you will learn how to target an RSSI floor for voice and how to reduce AP power to create smaller cells for dense areas. These outcomes reduce time, cost, and rework when you move to physical installation. Think about a recent site where a wall or shelving unit was unexpected — practicing these objectives helps you catch those issues in advance.

This second objectives screen focuses on applying the predictive survey skills and interpreting outputs. You will learn to place virtual APs both for coverage and for capacity-driven designs, and to use heatmaps for RSSI, SNR and throughput to check whether performance targets are met. For coverage-driven placement, the goal is a minimum RSSI target across the service area, for example a value suitable for voice. For capacity-driven placement you will learn to create smaller cells by reducing transmit power and placing APs closer together, which helps in high-density rooms such as conference spaces. You will also practice basic channel planning rules such as non-overlapping channels in 2.4 GHz and mindful channel separation and DFS considerations in 5 GHz. Finally, you will validate your design iteratively: place APs, generate heatmaps, inspect for red zones, and refine until the simulated results meet requirements. Knowing how to interpret SNR and throughput prevents common mistakes where good RSSI does not mean good performance. Consider which area in your environment needs capacity rather than simple coverage; that distinction guides AP count and placement.

A predictive site survey is a software-driven simulation that models Wi‑Fi signal propagation using a scaled floor plan and material attenuation values. The technique lets you approximate where signal will reach, how strong it will be, and where capacity limits may appear, all before any hardware is installed. This matters because it reduces the expensive cycle of installing APs, testing, and reworking placement. A good predictive survey starts with accurate inputs: the scaled drawing and realistic attenuation settings for walls, glass, and metallic obstacles. For example, a drywall partition will typically attenuate a 5 GHz signal by only a few decibels, while a thick concrete wall can cause an order of magnitude more loss. A common misconception is to treat a predictive survey as a final truth rather than a model; it is a tool that is only as accurate as the data you provide. Use predictive surveys to estimate AP count, initial placement, and where to focus a follow-up physical verification. In practice this means you can identify likely red zones on a heatmap, refine AP locations or power, and produce a design that requires fewer on-site adjustments. Ask yourself: what local construction features could change the model’s accuracy at your site?

Importing and scaling a floor plan is the foundation of every predictive survey. Begin by obtaining the best available drawing: a CAD file or a high-resolution image. When you import the file into survey software, you must set the real-world scale by measuring a known dimension on the plan, such as a 10 meter exterior wall, and inputting that length so the software can convert pixels or drawing units to meters. The guidance in the source material is clear: check at least two known distances after scaling to confirm accuracy. Common mistakes include using an unscaled or low-resolution image and assuming the drawing is to scale without verifying. Always validate your scale by measuring two independent dimensions—this catches distortions or different drawing scales across floors. If you discover errors, re-import or correct the scale before placing any virtual APs, since AP separation, coverage predictions, and channel planning depend on true distances. Finally, label key rooms and features so you can later map capacity requirements to specific areas. After scaling correctly, you can draw walls and obstacles and begin assigning material properties with confidence. What two distances can you verify on your next plan?

Material attenuation is the reduction in RF signal strength as radio waves pass through walls, glass, doors, furniture, or metallic structures. Different materials produce different losses. The chapter gives useful examples: a drywall office partition may attenuate a 5 GHz signal by around 3 to 5 dB, while a thick concrete wall often causes 10 to 15 dB loss. The hands-on scenario uses 12 dB for an exterior concrete wall and 4 dB for a drywall partition to illustrate how these values affect coverage predictions. It’s important to choose values that match local construction practices and, when possible, validate them with physical measurements. In survey software you typically draw walls and assign a material type from a library or custom values. A common misconception is to assume all walls are the same; a reinforced concrete shear wall can create a major coverage gap if modeled as a light partition. Another pitfall is to ignore metallic obstructions like shelving or elevator shafts which can present very high attenuation. Accurate material mapping helps your model reveal where extra APs will actually be needed rather than guessing later on-site. Which material near your site could change a predicted heatmap the most?

After scaling the floor plan, the next step is to draw and tag the building elements that affect radio propagation. Draw exterior and interior walls, doors, windows, elevator shafts and large metallic fixtures, then assign the material type and its attenuation value. This may be done by selecting a wall tool and tracing each wall segment to match the plan. Be deliberate: a missing shear wall or metallic storage rack can produce large unpredicted losses. Also include doors and glass where their lower attenuation impacts the heatmap. Many survey tools provide a library of materials with default dB losses; use these as a starting point but adjust to reflect local building practice — the chapter warns that regional construction differences matter. After drawing, run an initial simulation to confirm the heatmap behavior looks sensible: broad open areas should show larger coverage footprints, and thick walls should create distinct signal shadows. If results look implausible, re-check scale and material assignments. This step bridges the static floor plan and the dynamic RF model; accuracy here is what lets you trust subsequent AP placement and capacity estimates. Which structural element on your plan would you mark first and why?

Coverage-driven placement aims to ensure a minimum RSSI across the desired coverage area. Start by defining your RSSI target, for example a value suitable for voice, and then place virtual access points to meet that floor. After placing an AP, the software will generate a heatmap showing predicted RSSI; use that to identify areas below the target. Adjust AP location and transmit power to expand coverage where needed. A common mistake is to rely solely on transmit power increases to reach a distant area; this can create greater cell overlap and increase co-channel interference. Instead, move APs or add another AP in problem areas if the building structure blocks signals. For open areas you can often achieve coverage with fewer APs, while partitioned spaces may require additional APs near high-attenuation walls. The chapter emphasizes iterative refinement: place APs, check heatmaps, refine positions, and repeat until the coverage target is met without excessive overlap. Remember to keep SNR and throughput considerations in mind — good RSSI alone is not the whole picture. After you think coverage is solved, generate SNR and throughput heatmaps to verify real-world usability.

Coverage-driven and capacity-driven placement address different problems. Coverage placement aims for signal everywhere by meeting a minimum RSSI, useful in general office spaces or hallways. Capacity placement focuses on areas with many concurrent users where throughput per user matters, such as conference rooms. For capacity, you often place multiple APs closer together and reduce their transmit power to create smaller cells. This allows more APs to operate in proximity without overwhelming co-channel interference and helps distribute clients across access points. The chapter highlights that capacity-driven designs require careful attention to power and channel planning, and that tools can accept client density inputs to optimize AP count. A common error is to rely on a single AP to cover a dense area simply because its RSSI meets the target; in that case throughput and client distribution will suffer. Another pitfall is over-designing: too many APs can increase co-channel interference and reduce overall performance. The right strategy balances cell size, transmit power, and channel separation to meet both coverage and capacity where they matter most. Which of your spaces is likely to need capacity-focused placement?

Channel planning reduces co-channel interference and improves overall network performance. In 2.4 GHz the standard practice is to use the three non-overlapping channels — 1, 6 and 11 — to avoid adjacent-channel overlap. In 5 GHz and 6 GHz there are many more channels available, but you still need to ensure sufficient channel separation and be mindful of DFS channel behavior. The survey software typically provides initial channel assignment suggestions during predictive placement, but you should review and adjust them based on AP density and expected client channel use. A simple pitfall is to assume more APs means you can ignore channel planning; in fact, more APs make proper channel separation more important. When you design capacity-driven areas with smaller cells, lower transmit power helps, but you must coordinate channel assignments carefully to avoid multiple APs on the same channel in overlapping cells. Keep in mind that predictive tools can estimate interference but they cannot predict every external source — plan for some on-site verification and tuning after deployment. First, a predictive site survey models RF propagation with scaled floor plans and material attenuation so you can plan AP placement before installing hardware. Second, floor plan scaling is critical: set the scale using a known dimension and verify with at least one additional check to prevent distance errors. Third, material attenuation must be assigned thoughtfully — drywall has a small dB loss while concrete and metallic obstructions cause much larger losses that create coverage shadows. These concepts form the backbone of accurate predictive modeling. Memorize them as a sequence: scale, map materials, place APs, then analyze heatmaps. Following that sequence helps you catch the biggest errors early and focus your design efforts on the inputs that matter most. As you work through real sites, use these core ideas as a quick checklist before you trust simulated outputs.

Finish with three practical reminders. First, virtual AP placement must reflect your objectives: coverage-driven designs meet an RSSI floor while capacity-driven designs create smaller cells and distribute client load. Second, heatmaps are multidimensional: always consult RSSI, SNR and throughput together because each tells a different part of the performance story. Third, channel planning and avoiding over-design are crucial — adding APs without channel coordination can increase co-channel interference and harm throughput. These reminders help you translate predictive outputs into deployable designs. When a problem appears on a heatmap, prefer targeted AP placement changes rather than blunt power increases, and always schedule an on-site verification to compare model predictions with measured results. Keep this practical checklist handy while you plan: scale correctly, model materials properly, choose placement strategy intentionally, check heatmaps comprehensively, and verify on site.
